clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Gordon's stroke in June 1991, within the next three years: your wrist injury stopped your playing and your anxiety rose; you and Rafe had a blow-up and he moved out; you were on your own, getting high, absorbed in fixing radios; you felt lost and low, unable to get going, with your grandfather gone and your mother about to remarry; your grandmother Winifred was treated for a thyroid tumour within a year or so of being widowed; a bleak year at community college followed, nights out playing pool, days asleep; your parents married in the autumn of 1992; your father was stung that he had never heard of the film you were making, and you leaned toward him; an exchange in Lisbon then Porto turned things around and you raced through the rest of your degree. Your cousin Bella was treated for melanoma in 1994, around the same time. The shifts pile up from your first term away through your settling into study again, each one touching on your own troubles or those close by; no one else's shifts show in these months.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's death, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Winifred found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, within the next two years: you were running out of steam for performing and your anxiety rose; you had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra and your functioning fell; you were on poor terms with family and friends, and you kept your distance from your parents; you left Thornbury for Gull Harbour; you met Marisol at a winter party and moved to Fenwick to live with her; you split up within the year; you sank into a deep depression once you split, and returned to Thornbury; your parents seemed a world away from what you were going through, and you could not face them; you relied on friends, gingerly, bunking with Corbin and Dale then Hamish; you dropped in briefly on her sickroom hung over on the way to the airport, your last visit; she died of bowel cancer in February 2004. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home. Your anxiety rose and you kept your distance as the months wore on; your functioning fell through the depression and began to lift once you requested help with therapy costs and returned to your therapist. The trouble reaches from before the diagnosis through to the months after her death, when you began swimming laps and moved toward your therapist and your parents again.
